questions.questionText: Bring out the causes of persistent high food inflation in India and suggest measures for ensuring long-  term price stability.

answers.answerText:
| **Approach:** • Introduce the answer by defining inflation and giving a brief background of the persistent high food inflation in India.
• In the body, first bring out the causes for the same.
• Next, suggest measures for ensuring long term price stability.
• Conclude by emphasizing their synergy and link to SDGs. | | --- | **Inflation** is the **rate of increase in prices** of goods and services in an economy over a given period of time. Economic Survey (2024-25) points out the **persistence in inflation**, particularly food inflation. Food inflation **surged after the pandemic** to 6.4 per cent on average (between 2020-21 and 2023-24), higher than the 5.9 per cent overall CPI inflation. **Fig. Comparison of retail and food inflation** (Jan 2024-Jan 2025). Experts have cited the **following factors** as being responsible for the **persistent high food inflation** in India: 1. a) rise in prices of **vegetables and pulses** which combinedly hold a high **weightage** (8.99%) in overall CPI basket; b) increase in **international prices** of cereals (wheat) and **fertilizers** due to the impact of **geopolitical conflicts** (Russia-Ukraine war). 2. a) Lower harvest in **price-sensitive commodities** (onion) in major **producing regions** (Maharashtra, Rajasthan, Gujarat) due to **uneven monsoon**; b) damage to **horticultural crops** due to **unseasonal** **pre-monsoonal rainfall,** which also trigger **temporary storage and transportation problems**. 3. a) Highly **perishable** nature of certain commodities (tomato); b) **temporal and spatial** concentration of production (tur dal in Maharashtra and Karnataka) makes it susceptible to **regional issues and** **supply chain** constraints; c) **limited potential for import** during periods of shortage due to India’s status as a **major producer** (pointed out by Economic Survey 2024-25). Ensuring **long-term price stability** India requires a mix of **following** measures such as:. 1. **Controlling artificial scarcity:** a) prevent hoarding by strengthening **Essential Commodities Act,** b) strict enforcement of **stock limits** c) improve **real-time price monitoring** using digital tools. 2. **Enhancing productivity:** a) promoting **high-yield seeds, precision farming, efficient irrigation** (drip, sprinkler) b) **crop diversification (**crop rotation, intercropping) for risk sharing. c) expand **storage** **infrastructure** to reduce post-harvest losses d) Strengthening **food processing capabilities (**PM FME) to stabilize supply throughout the year. 3. **Reforming agricultural market:** a) strengthening **e-NAM** to ensure better price discovery b) expanding **DBT** for fertilizers subsidies to reduce production cost c) flexible **MSP and procurement** **policy** that adjusts to production levels d) exploring a **stable agri-EXIM policy regime** to ensure sustained availability of products. Managing persistent high food inflation requires **comprehensive measures** including **supply-side** **interventions, market reforms**, and **sustainable agriculture** to balance consumer affordability with farm income stability. ***(401 words)***

questions.questionText: “Fiscal policy can serve as a cornerstone for sustainable development”. In light of this statement,  discuss the significance of fiscal policy in a developing economy like India.

answers.answerText:
| **Approach:** • Introduce the answer by defining fiscal policy.
• In the body, discuss the significance of fiscal policy in a developing economy like India.
• Conclude by highlighting the importance of deficit management and coordination with monetary policy for sustainable development. | | --- | Fiscal policy refers to the government's use of **expenditure and revenue measures** to influence various aspects of the national economy- levels of **economic activity, employment, price stability,** etc. In a developing country like India, fiscal policy holds **immense significance**, especially in **ensuring** **sustainable development,** as discussed: 1. Enhancing people’s **disposable incomes** and **standard of living** through **wealth redistribution** and reducing **income inequality. (SDG 10)** a. **Income support** schemes (PM-KISAN) and provision of b**asic goods and services** through dedicated schemes (PMAY, NFSA). b. a) Reduction in **personal income taxes**; b) **progressive taxation** policies (higher proportion of direct tax) and generational **wealth redistribution** (wealth tax, inheritance tax); c) access to **basic** **goods and services** (lower GST on items of mass consumption). 2. Provides fiscal stimulation and enhances **economic competitiveness** through infrastructural and industrial development (**SDG 9**). a. a) Capital expenditure** (11,11,111cr for 2024-25) creates a crowd**-in effec**t for private investment;** b) support for the **manufacturing sector** (PLIs) and enhancing **job creation** (ELIs) c) **strategic disinvestment policy** to optimize **resource allocation** (Air India, BPCL disinvestment) and improve **efficiency**. b. a) Tax incentives** for **infrastructure development** (Section 80IA deductions, infrastructure bond benefits);** b) **targeted tax measures** to boost industrial growth (corporate tax cuts) and **entrepreneurship** (abolition of angel tax); c) **infrastructure-specific levies** (infrastructure cess) to fund development projects. 3. Provision for **social support system. (SDG 3,4,6):** a. a) Expenditure on **public health** infrastructure, **education** infrastructure (PM-Shri Schools) leading to better health (reduced MMR) and education outcomes (near 100% GER in primary education); b) **social security** through dedicated schemes (NSAP, One Rank One Pension). b. a) Building **health and education services** (health and education cess); b) allocation from the **Universal Service Obligation Fund** to improve **digital infrastructure** and connectivity in underserved areas. 4. Furthering **inclusive growth** and **human development**. (**SDG 1,2,6**) a. a) **Gender equity** through gender-responsive budgeting and supportive institutions (One Stop Centres) b) empowerment of **vulnerable sections** of society (PM JANMAN) c) **poverty alleviation** measures (MGNREGA) and schemes for **nutritional security** (PM POSHAN). b. a) Tax incentives for women** (lower stamp duty on women owned properties);** b) agricultural promotion by **exempting agricultural income** from tax. 5. Promote **desirable consumption** patterns to achieve **sustainable growth**. (**SDG 7,11,12**) a. a) Access to **clean energy** sources (PM Ujjwala Yojana; PM Surya Ghar Bijli), reducing **carbon** **footprint** (FAME scheme). b. a) **Sin tax** on energy generation from fossil fuels (clean energy cess on coal); b) **excise and** **customs relief** to increase availability of components for renewable energy projects (solar panels); c) **green financing instruments** (Green Bonds). India's developmental journey (**Viksit Bharat 2047**) requires balancing **growth with equity**. Within a framework of **prudent deficit management** (FRBM Act), and complemented by appropriate **monetary policy**, fiscal measures create an **enabling environment** for **inclusive** and **sustainable development**. (***454 words***)

b) industrial growth provides jobs for **semi-skilled** and **unskilled** workers, promoting **inclusive growth**; c) helps in realizing India's **'demographic dividend'** by employing the large working-age population. 2. a) **Domestic manufacturing capabilities** in critical sectors (defense, pharmaceuticals, semiconductors, rare earth elements) reduce **dependence on imports** and vulnerability to global **supply chain disruptions;** b) strengthens **national security** and **economic sovereignty** by ensuring control over **strategic technologies** and resources. 3. a) Manufacturing creates crucial **forward and backward linkages**;
